rationale: The decision to switch the flag on depends on how often it misses urgent messages, which a diagnostic accuracy study answers: the flag runs silently, sampled messages are rated by two clinicians blind to the flag with third-clinician adjudication (c3), and accuracy is reported overall, by clinic and by language because it varies with population (c2, c4). The planning value for sensitivity comes from a primary care validation (c1).
alternatives: Switch the flag on and monitor (refused: misses would reach patients before accuracy is known)
Single-clinic study (refused: accuracy varies by clinic population)
Randomised comparison of flagged and unflagged queues (deferred: only after accuracy is acceptable)
whyNotMoreComplex: A randomised comparison of queues would expose patients to an unvalidated flag; accuracy comes first.

decision.statement: Run a multi-clinic diagnostic accuracy study of the flag in silent mode against an adjudicated two-clinician reference standard, with random sampling and results by clinic and message language.
decision.question: Should the organisation switch on the automated urgent-message flag?

criteria.text: Sensitivity varies by clinic population, so local multi-site accuracy is needed.
A reliable reference standard can be built with adjudication.

gates.requirement: Privacy approval for extracting message text
gates.evidence: Privacy office approval PRV-2026-221 dated 2026-09-15, supplied by the investigator

gates.requirement: Vendor agreement to run the flag in silent mode
gates.evidence: Vendor agreement VEN-2026-09, supplied by the investigator

decision.note: Rests on ledger claims c1, c3 and c4 from retrieved records; both gates rest on investigator-supplied approvals.

summary: Diagnostic accuracy study recommended; decision rests on three ledger claims; gates met.
